entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-11-15
entry.content:
Nvidia remained the background question, now as "buy the dip" and "is circular financing bad" threads ahead of the 17 November results. The specific material was elsewhere: Berkshire priced its yen bonds, and careful pitches with stated assumptions on CATL, Deckers, Wise and Lululemon drew comments that tested them. The top-scoring post, a link calling staples the real bubble, had no argument attached beyond its comments.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-11-12
entry.content:
Nvidia dominated again. Over three days the question moved from whether the board investigation deserved a discount to whether Nvidia at "around 10x" forward earnings is a value stock, and the run ended with Huang's resignation, which the threads read had not yet caught up with. The other material worth reading was Costco's $30 special dividend, which the sub turned into an argument about paying a high multiple for predictability, plus asset-based pitches for Macy's and Weyerhaeuser and a worked note on Bogle's return formula.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-11-09
entry.content:
Over the weekend the sub turned to Nvidia's governance. Its board opened an independent investigation into Jensen Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and three threads asked whether this should cost Nvidia anything in its valuation. The more useful material was Berkshire's Q3 results, which landed alongside a thread testing a price-to-book "buyback line", plus pushback on a semiconductor memo and on pitches for Pepsi, McCormick and ServiceNow.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-11-06
entry.content:
This run came the day after a sharp sell-off on 5 November, which coverage blames on a Democratic midterm sweep and fears of data-centre restrictions. Most of the hot list reacted to it: "Why Is the Stock Market Getting Destroyed Today?" (310 points), "What are you buying today?" and a 296-point post calling Nvidia a bargain at 13x forward earnings. The best material was the pushback on that post, a long Uber pitch with a reply that challenges its free-cash-flow figure, and a backtest of seven value screens run under the same conditions.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-11-01
entry.content:
This run came after the sell-off. Most of the hot list was dip-buying questions ("What dips are you buying?", "Which Mag-7 offers the best value?"), and a 333-point post told members who panic over red days to leave. Reddit (the company) drew three posts after what one poster calls a 29% fall on 30 October, and the best reply among them used the filed numbers to ask what the bull case depends on. Alphabet came back as a $601 "fair value" model that the comments took apart. The one live corporate action was a member's holding, High Liner Foods, being bought out.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-29
entry.content:
Alphabet's results took over the run. The 471-point "Can we shut up about GOOG finally?" and four other Google threads argued about one quarter, and the filed release settles most of the factual disputes in them, including the corrections. The second-most-upvoted thread was a Meta Muse product test (464 points), which is a user review, not an analysis. The smaller useful material: a Sprouts reply that caught a 53-week-year adjustment in the guidance, a reverse-DCF Reddit pitch with a good methodological objection, and Anthropic's S-1, which is now public.

Read the full run

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-26
entry.content:
This was a pre-earnings run. Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft report this week and SoFi on Tuesday, and the biggest threads were "Is GOOGL a buy?" (216 points), "One stock for 10 years" (174) and a Netflix bear-case request (144) — questions rather than arguments. The useful material is smaller. A Nike-versus-Pepsi yield post had a commenter who opened Nike's 10-K, and a SoFi post asked how much of its tangible book is fair-value marks. Both are checking methods that work beyond the one stock. Netflix's own letter confirms the figures in both Netflix threads, and Lula's runoff win landed on MercadoLibre after the scan's snapshot was taken. Last run's unsourced claim about Sea insider selling now has filings-based coverage behind it.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-23
entry.content:
This was a Meta earnings run: three of the sub's threads were about the same quarter, and the two best-sourced things in it are a share class nobody read the filing on and a $25 billion judgment the sub mentioned once, in passing, under a thread about Alphabet. Both Must know stories are therefore Meta's, which is lopsided and also what the run was. Below that, the useful material is a reverse-DCF Adobe memo whose own author wrote the sharpest reply in the thread, a 13-quarter normalisation that dismantles the run's "AI made Meta efficient" post, and a reminder that the sub is still working from CoreWeave's wrong debt figure three days after this feed checked the filing. The sub's single most popular post was downvoted in its own comments for calling this a value investor's market.

Read the full run

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-20
entry.content:
The sub's attention split this run between one unusually popular curiosity and the same AI-credit argument it has been having for a fortnight. Tootsie Roll at 714 points was the biggest thread the feed has seen in weeks, and two of its three headline facts do not survive the balance sheet. The AI threads produced something better than last run: a post that went to CoreWeave's 10-Q rather than to the viral bond yield, and a data-centre IPO post whose list of pulled and repriced floats checks out line by line. The best-sourced small threads were a FICO fund-letter compilation quoting five managers verbatim, an Alcoa write-up whose bear case got challenged on the right number, and a Q3 insider-trading post sitting at 1 point whose filings all check out. Two Must know stories passed the test.

Read the full run

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-17
entry.content:
Almost every large thread this run was about one thing: whether the credit markets are right about AI infrastructure. CoreWeave's bond yields, Anthropic's finances, the Gartner impairment report and Nvidia's vendor financing drew four of the five biggest discussions, and in three of them the sub was arguing from a figure that is wrong or half-quoted. The best-sourced small threads were elsewhere: an Embecta pitch that names its own bear case, a Deckers write-up whose comments attacked the arithmetic rather than the brands, and a Berkshire valuation post with no replies at all that rebuilt look-through earnings from scratch. Two Must know stories passed the test, both corrections.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-14
entry.content:
The run was dominated by "cheap on every metric and still a bad buy", a 238-comment value-trap thread whose answers were mostly Nike, and by the sub's unease about how much of its own attention AI has taken. The two best-sourced threads were small: a Group 1 Automotive post whose activist story is three filings out of date, and a JPMorgan earnings-call diff whose numbers mostly check out and whose three misses are worth knowing. One Must know story passed the test this run; the Hemnet and Palantir pitches were the only others that showed their assumptions.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-11
entry.content:
Two outside events drove the sub this run: SpaceX's low-band spectrum deal, which sent the US telcos down, and American Express's $350 million anti-money-laundering penalty. The pitches were almost all "the market has mistaken a slowdown for an ending" — Deckers, Baidu, D'Ieteren, Intuit and RELX — and the loudest thread of the run was an ex-Adobe engineer arguing the opposite about Adobe. No new filed moves by well-known investors appeared.

entry.title: Value investing digest, 2026-10-08
entry.content:
The top thread was Berkshire's latest Lennar purchases. Most of the rest was beaten-down names: European holding companies and real estate, a Stellantis turnaround, Uber's exposure to self-driving cars, and stocks sold off on AI fears. The best threads were about method: when to sell, and what a DCF is really saying when almost all of its value sits after year five.
